sections.heading: Monument-
sections.content: Literally meaning rock-cave, there are four important Tak-Phu of special importance, one in each direction. These are four sacred caves where Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava or the Second Buddha) and Lhatsun Chhembo are said to have halted and meditated. These are namely Lha-ri nying phu, Kah-do Sang phu, Pe-phu and De-chhen phu.

sections.heading: Interesting facts
sections.content: Monasteries are mostly known as Gompas. But Gompa literally means "a place of solitude", a religious escape where monks are iner aspects of Tibetan Buddhism. Most gompas in Sikkim are found in solitary places since isolation from the world has always been an important aspect of Buddhist learning merely as an escape from worldly temptations. Monasteries usually occupy commanding and frequently picturesque sites. The monastic buildings cluster around the main building which is also used as the Assembly Hall or du-khang. Rows of prayer flags and chortens are lined up along the path to Gompa.

sections.heading: Sikkim- Monument- Monasteries - Rumtek Gompa
sections.content: Back in the 1950s when the Chinese invaded Tibet, His Holiness, the Gyalwa Karmapa  the sixteenth Karmapa and head of the Kagyu-pa (Black Hat) order of Buddhism, came to live in Sikkim. In the 1960s, he constructed the three-storeyed Rumtek Gompa. It is believed that the monastery is an excellent replica of the original Kagyu-pa Monastery in Tsurphu, Tibet. It remains the biggest monastery in Sikkim, and is a fine example of Tibetan architecture. The latest Karmapa who fled Tibet in the year 2000, now resides in the Rumtek Gompa. It of the world's most unique religious scriptures, manuscripts and religious art objects. The large prayer-hall in the monastery is especially noteworthy for its exquisite murals, statues and tangkhas (painted or embroidered scrolls).

sections.heading: Sikkim- Monument- Monasteries - Labrang Gompa
sections.content: The Labrang Gompa, which belongs to the Nyingmapa (Red Hat) Order of Buddhism is a monastery which was built about a 100 years after the Phodang Gompa. From the monastery one can see the ruins of the third capital of Sikkim Tumlong, which became the capital in the early nineteenth century and remained so for about 90 years. Only the chortens (a dome-shaped structure that contains the relics of the Buddha or other Buddhist saints) that surround the palace are still somewhat recognizable.

sections.heading: Sikkim- Monument-
sections.content: The most powerful monastery of the Nyingmapa Order of Buddhism in Sikkim is the Pemayangste Gompa, also considered by many as the premier house of faith in Sikkim. Situated at a great height, the gompa offers spectacular views of the surrounding landscape. Founded in 1705, Pemayangste, or the Perfect Sublime Lotus is also one of the oldest monasteries in the state, and has been reconstructed several times. The gompa is a three-storeyed structure and contains numerous antique idols and objects of worship and is filled with wall paintings and sculptures. A stand-out feature of the Monastery is a seven-tiered painted wooden structure on the top floor portraying the Guru Rimpoches Heavenly Palace Santopalri which was completed single handedly by the late Dungzin Rimpoche in a span of five years.

sections.heading: Monument-
sections.content: The Tashiding Gompa, believed to be amongst the most sacred monasteries in Sikkim. Founded in 1717, the gompa crowns the top of a hill that is sandwiched between the Rathong and the Rangeet Rivers. Perhaps its awesome location has something to do with the local belief, according to which the mere sight of the Tashiding Gompa cleanses one of all sins. The pretty structure with its many colourful flags fluttering in the wind seems straight out of a picture postcard. The monasterys vivid Bumchu festival, takes place every year in the month of March.

sections.heading: Carpet Weaving
sections.content: The women of Sikkim practice what is perhaps the oldest form of carpet weaving in the world. The tradition is essentially Central Asian and a frame loom is used for the purpose. The women of the Bhutia community are believed to be expert weavers. The warp is prepared from cotton and is stretched on a frame. Different colors of wool are introduced into the pattern and so are a number of rods. The patterns commonly woven onto the carpets are a dragon holding a ball in his mouth or stylized floral motifs. Patterns are based on Buddhist motifs and figures. Geometrical patterns are popular too. Most patterns draw heavily on the surrounding beauty of the landscape.

sections.heading: Sikkim- Handicrafts- Wood Carving
sections.content: Monasteries and many buildings in Sikkim are richly decorated with symbols and icons. These symbols are painted or embossed on the walls or on thangkas (paintings), or depicted in the exquisite woodcarvings that adorn these monasteries. Sikkims famous mask dances also display the expertise of the locals with wood. Costumed Lamas with gaily painted masks, ceremonial swords and sparkling jewels, leap and swing to the rhythm of resounding drums, trumpeting of horns and chanting of monks. The hand made masks they wear are either of wooden or of papier-mâché. Many monasteries are also decorated with wooden carvings. For instance, the Pemayangtse monastery, surrounded by mountains, glaciers and passes, has a number of elegantly carved wooden sculptures.

sections.heading: Sikkim- Handicrafts- Thangka Paintings
sections.content: Known as thangkas, the typical paintings of Sikkim, were originally a medium of reverence through which the highest ideals of Buddhism were evoked. Thangkas are created on cotton canvas and often framed with silk. They depict images of different gods, goddesses, and philosophies related to Buddhism. Traditionally, thangkas were made by Buddhist priests and monks and some specific ethnic groups. The skills were passed from generation to generation. The art has also helped the monasteries and its practitioners keep it alive. There are three types of thangkas. One depicts the life of Buddha, his birth, his disillusionment with life, his search for enlightenment and his understanding of life. The second type of thangka is more abstract and represents the Buddhist beliefs of life and death. One example could be the Tibetan Wheel of Life, which symbolizes the Buddhist belief of transmigratory existence. The third type of the thangka consists of paintings that are often used as a tool for meditation or as offerings to the deities. These paintings are usually done against a white background. The colors used are all vegetable dyes and each has a special significance. White stands for serenity, golden for the birth or life, enlightenment, and parinirvana, red for the intensity of passion both love and hatred, black for anger, yellow for compassion and green for consciousness. The colors used in making a thangka are all vegetable or mineral dyes extracted from nature.

sections.heading: Sikkim- Handicrafts- Handlooms
sections.content: The traditional Sikkimese weaves and woolen blankets which can be designed into bags, shawls, jackets, opulent Sikkimese thangkas (traditional tapestry), leather works, dolls, variegated applique work, batiks, an exquisite selection of dolls and a variety of fashionable garments for modern people are the other specialties of the state.
